messages.subject: pooling survey data when replicate transects lines varied in
messages.subject_clean: pooling survey data when replicate transects lines varied in
messages.body_plain:
I'm having trouble deciding how to pool data from transects in a
multi-year aerial survey of bottlenose dolphins.  Our data consists of
perpendicular distances from transects lines flown across a 250 km-long
lagoonal system.  We did repeated samples within seasons for several
years (semi-monthly for 2 years, and monthly the last year) but need to
pool data temporally due to low numbers of sightings on any given sample
day.  During the first two years (study 1), on each survey date we
randomly picked 1 among 5 transects within each of 46 equidistant zones
arranged along the long-axis of the lagoon.  During the last year (study
2) we fixed the transects within the 46 zones and repeated them on each
survey.

My questions are:
1) During both studies, we recorded the actual lengths flown for each
transect during each survey, using a GPS.  Thus, our replicate transects
lines actually had different lengths on the different surveys, due to
the ability of our pilot to get on the exact coordinates of the line.  I
realize that this happens at some scale on all surveys, but the
difference we measured was typically several hundred meters (average
transect length was around 3 km, thus roughly 10% difference between
surveys) .  Should we fix the transect length and use that rather than
using the exact distance covered during each individual survey?  Or is
there a way to reflect this difference in effort while retaining the
appropriate unit of replication for estimating the encounter rate
variance.

2) During study 1, for which we used the randomization to pick 1 among 5
transects within each zone, when we subsequently pool the data, should
we treat the lines that were repeated as replicates? My concern is that
in addition to problem 1 (above), this will occur in an unbalanced
fashion due to having different numbers of replicates for the various
transect lines?  For example, over the course of 45 surveys, transect
13a may have been covered 20 times while 13b was covered 5 times, 13c 15
times, 13d 3 times, and 13e 3 times.  The alternative is to treat the
transect lines within each survey as unique.  Thus in the example, we
would have 46 different lines within that zone.  I'm worried about bias
in the estimate of encounter rate variance.  I'm wondering if there is
another way to structure the data to allow for some replication within
this study design?

Eric D. Stolen, Ph.D.
Dynamac Corp.

Kennedy Space Center, FL  32899

messages.subject: Re: pooling survey data when replicate transects lines varied in
messages.subject_clean: pooling survey data when replicate transects lines varied in
messages.body_plain:
With the scale at which you are working I'd be surprised to see much of
a difference regardless of the way that you handled it.  That said, what
is not clear to me is what temporal scale you want to use for estimation
of abundance.  Is it monthly or annually?  Also you typically don't need
to pool the data for estimation of the encounter rate.  The pooling is
done to provide adequate estimation of detection probability and with
the scale of your survey you should consider using covariates to account
for changes in detection probability. The advice given in the book of
visiting the same lines on multiple surveys is intended for the
situation to boost the number of detections in a small area,  animal
distribution is not changing much at all and density is constant so a
single estimate is the goal.  From your description you have 46 lines
per survey which is more than adequate to estimate the average encounter
rate and it's variance for each monthly or semi-monthly survey.
However, if you do use covariates or  pool detections to estimate
detection probability that will induce covariance between your
estimates.  With regard to your specific questions you should definitely
use the distance travelled rather than planned distance but be careful
of using GPS positions taken too frequently in time.  Even with the
higher accuracy you can achieve with GPS these days there is error
associated with the lines and if you take a position say every 1 sec the
error can mount up quickly creating an apparent jagged "longer" line
from what was a flown straight line.  With regard to imbalance of effort
from number of times sampling a line, that is not problematic as long as
you define effort to be length of the line times the frequency it was
sampled.  However, that approach would only be necessary if you were
only interested in an average annual estimate and you thought that the
population moved very little relative to the line spacing.  The latter
seems unlikely with bottlenose dolphins in the lagoon system.  Given
what little I know about these dolphins I'd think you'ld want to create
monthly estimates of abundance and use covariates for detection
probability.  You can do that by using the mrds engine in D5 (for a
single platform) and define months as strata and each strata would use
the total area of the lagoon.  It will provide the estimates per month
and their covariances.  The total it provides is nonsense in that case
although if you divide that estimate and std error by the number of
strata (months) it will provide the average abundance and its precision.

hope this helps --jeff

messages.subject: Primate census in small areas
messages.body_plain:
Hi List,

I have some questions about how to design a survey for primates in a small
area. Cocha Cashu Biological Station has a net of trails inside an area of
10 square kilometers. It is very hard to build several long transects, but
it is possible to build a lot of short transects, then, what is more
important: line length or number of transects? If I have to use many short
transects, and I want to calculate the density of primates just in the dry
season of one year. do I have to walk any transect several times or just
once? The "effort" concept is not very clear for me.

Monkeys don't use trails, I think there is no bias generated because the
trail system, or not?

Thanks for your time.

N.

--

messages.subject: Re: stratification
messages.body_plain:
Hi Roberta, List,

It is not clear from your description, but I take it that you had=20
transects laid in each habitat (woodland and field), so each transect is=20
either along one or the other, but in some cases you detected animals in=20
say a field (presumably away from the line) when doing a woodland=20
transect - if that is the case the cross-classified individuals are=20
always at larger distances.

If that is the case, just follow your design: do an analysis stratified=20
by habitat type (potentially both detection function and density might=20
be different by habitat), i.e., for the strata definition you ignore=20
where the animal was, and use only where the transect was. If you do=20
that, probably using or not the animals say seen in field when doing a=20
woodland analysis (and vice versa - assuming these are not a "large"=20
proportion of the observations, with "large" vaguely defined here...)=20
will have a minor impact any way (removing them just means you lower the=20
detection probability away from the line, and that should be fine -=20
estimation of density is still unbiased given everything else is OK).=20
With such different habitats, detection should be different by habitat,=20
but you can use AIC to see if a pooled detection function might be adequa=
te.

Note that if you use a separate detection by stratum, you should not use=20
the habitat the animal was in as a covariate, because there is no=20
independence between the covariate value and distance (here I'm=20
assuming, as I said above, that if  you have a detection function for=20
each habitat stratum, in each stratum the animals observed in the other=20
habitat will all be at large distances).

Hope this helps,

Tiago

messages.subject: proper sampling unit for stratified design
messages.subject_clean: proper sampling unit for stratified design
messages.body_plain:
Hi Distance Samplers,

I'm working with some bird point transect data collected in oak woodlands. The
survey design was as follows: 91 points were clustered within 16 "Units"
representing either untreated or treated woodlands (treatment involved
understory removal), and the points were surveyed twice in each of two
consecutive years. Units averaged 21 hectares and were not physically connected
to each other. I'll ultimately need density estimates for several species in
each stratum (treated  and untreated) in each year. This will likely require
stratum estimates to often be based on pooled detection functions due to small
numbers of detections per stratum.

The folks I'm working with are concerned that using the individual points as the
sampling unit amounts to pseudoreplication, and that perhaps data from all
points in a unit should be pooled, with "Unit" (n=16) as the sampling unit. The
encounter rates and density estimates don't differ when I use this approach,
but, as you would expect, the variances are much higher, often twice as high (CV
of 40+ versus 20+). This is true for global as well as stratum estimates.

So is this pooling necessary, I'm wondering? Or is it a bit overcautious,
statistically speaking?

Mark Faherty
Ecostudies Institute
Homestead, FL
USA

--
